citation: Farmers' perceptions of stock theft in South Africa (PLOS ONE, 2024)
Welfare impact of stock theft, Nyandeni (SciELO SA, 2025)
mechanisms: Livestock is a high-value, movable target that is easy to convert into cash or cultural goods, so theft becomes a rational choice whenever guardianship is absent.
When herding labour is unaffordable and grazing camps are distant, livestock left unguarded become an open invitation to theft.
Lenient sentences signal that the state does not take livestock theft seriously, so only the threat of lifetime imprisonment is seen as a real deterrent.
Cultural ceremonies create a steady, unregulated demand for livestock that does not require proof of ownership, so theft surges around traditional events.
Without widespread branding or tattooing, stolen livestock become anonymous goods, making detection and recovery nearly impossible.
objection_patterns: How will this policy make it harder to sell stolen livestock at traditional events without a certificate of ownership?
How will this policy help me afford a herder when I am already struggling to get by?
How will this policy make the punishment harsh enough that thieves actually fear it?
How will this policy help me identify my animals when they are taken far away in the dark?
confidence: Mixed-methods and review-based, two-study synthesis covering Eastern Cape communal areas — mechanisms are well-attested in participant perception, but magnitudes and causal weights are not quantified.
